result.reason: The passage directly defines the two hybrid cases (lishmo/shelo lishmo and shelo lishmo/lishmo) with the Pesach/shelamim examples, which is precisely what the 'Mixed Intentions' prose section describes and sets up.

The passage is Rav Pappa's dilemma about whether the mishna's mixed intentions (lishmo and shelo lishmo) refer to one rite or two, which directly follows the prose in candidate 5 that describes the mixed-intention cases and explicitly states 'how and when these two intentions occurred... is precisely the question the Gemara now takes up.'

The passage quotes Rabbi Yosei's principle that 'a person is held accountable even for the conclusion of his statement,' which is precisely what the prose of candidate 1 ('Rabbi Meir vs Yose') explains and discusses.

All three items together constitute the Gemara's clarification that the shelo lishmo u'lishmo case is not the interesting question (since everyone agrees it invalidates immediately), and that Rav Pappa's question must therefore be about lishmo u'shelo lishmo — which is precisely what the 'Shelo Lishmo First' prose section describes.

All 8 items form a continuous Gemara discussion attempting to determine which scenario the mishnah describes (one avodah vs. two avodot, Rabbi Meir vs. Rabbi Yosei), which matches candidate 1 ('Mishnah Interpretation') whose prose explicitly says 'The question is simply: which scenario does our mishnah actually describe? The Gemara will now attempt to resolve this through careful reading of the mishnah itself.'

The passage is the Gemara's attempt to prove from the seifa (the mishna about wrong owners/eaters) that the earlier mishna also concerns one avodah, which is precisely what the 'Proof from Seifa' prose describes.
The passage contains the Gemara's rebuttal 'ha kede'ita veha kede'ita' — each mishna operates on its own terms — which is precisely what the 'Separate Mishnas' prose describes.

All four items together form the Gemara's attempt to prove from the mishnah about le'ochlav ushelo le'ochlav — analyzing whether it refers to two avodot or one, concluding it must refer to one avodah, then inferring about the reisha, and finally rejecting that inference — which matches candidate 1's prose about this exact proof attempt from the owners' mishnah's positive case.

The passage asks precisely what happens when a Pesach designated before Pesach is slaughtered with a mixed intention (lishmo ushelo lishmo), which matches the 'Mixed on Purim' section's prose about the Gemara posing the question of a mixed intention on Purim for a designated Pesach.

Both items together form exactly the exchange described in the 'Rav Dimi Argument' prose — Rav Dimi's reasoning presented to Rabbi Yirmiyah and Rabbi Yirmiyah's rejection of it — which is precisely what that section's prose summarizes.

Both items present Rava's logical inference: since shelo lishmo overcomes the korban's own standing Pesach identity (stama lishmo ka'ei) in the undetermined case, it must equally prevail when both lishmo and shelo lishmo are stated explicitly — which is precisely the content of 'Rava's Logic' prose.

The passage contains Rav Adda bar Ahava's challenge to Rava distinguishing between cases where one explicitly says a hybrid intention versus cases where one says nothing and the korban's status fills in the gap, which is precisely what the prose under 'Speaking Weakness' (index 4) describes.

The passage is Rava's rejection of the comparison between the two cases ('Are the two cases comparable?'), which is precisely what candidate 4 ('Different Cases') describes — Rava rejecting the comparison and explaining the asymmetry between the eaters case and the Purim/purpose case.

The passage explains why the eaters case is different — because Paschal lamb subscribers can withdraw until slaughter, making the korban's status mutable — which directly supports Rava's distinction described in the 'Debate Ends' prose.
